name: The Ground
summary: Defines the field of play, its markings, and dimensions.
what_it_says: The field of play stretches up to 100 metres in length between goal lines, with in-goal areas of up to 22 metres behind each one, and is up to 70 metres wide. The pitch is marked with a halfway line, 22-metre lines, 5-metre and 10-metre lines, and touchlines along both sides.
why_it_exists: Every law that depends on distance, including offside lines, the 22, and the 50:22, only works if the pitch itself is standardised. This law is the foundation everything else is measured against.
in_practice: Commentators reference these lines constantly: found touch just inside the 22, kicked from inside his own half. Knowing the basic layout, with halfway and two 22s between two try lines, makes most other laws click into place faster, since so many of them describe positions relative to these markings.
common_confusions: The in-goal area isn't part of the field of play itself, it's additional space behind each try line where tries are scored. The field of play and the in-goal areas are measured and treated as separate zones.

name: Ball
summary: Defines the shape, size, and weight of the rugby ball used in matches.
what_it_says: The ball must be oval, made of four panels, and fall within a size and weight range set by World Rugby. Its irregular shape is what causes the unpredictable bounce rugby is known for.
why_it_exists: A standard ball means the game plays consistently wherever it's used, from a school pitch to a World Cup final. The oval shape is also central to the sport's identity, since passing, kicking, and catching an oval ball is a different skill entirely from a round one.
in_practice: Smaller ball sizes are used at junior levels to suit smaller hands, while professional and adult matches use a standard size. Weather affects handling more than in most sports because of the shape, since a wet ball is genuinely harder to catch and pass cleanly.
common_confusions: The odd bounce of the ball isn't just bad luck or poor handling. It's a direct, designed consequence of the oval shape, and turning that unpredictability to your advantage is part of the actual skill of the game.

name: Team
summary: Sets how many players each team fields, and how replacements and substitutions work.
what_it_says: A team fields 15 players in full XVs rugby, with a limited number of replacements permitted from the bench depending on the level of competition. Front-row replacements have specific minimum requirements, since scrums need suitably trained players in those positions for safety reasons.
why_it_exists: Limiting squad size and replacements keeps the contest fair and prevents teams from simply rotating in fresh legs indefinitely. The stricter front-row rules exist purely for safety, since an undertrained or fatigued front-row player in a scrum is a real injury risk to everyone bound in with them.
in_practice: Replacements typically come on for tactical reasons, like fresh legs late in the game, or for injury. If a team can't field enough front-row specialists due to injury or cards, scrums may have to go uncontested, which changes how that phase of the game is played for the rest of the match.
common_confusions: A red card doesn't necessarily mean a team plays permanently down a player in every competition. Some formats allow a replacement for the carded player after a set period of time, though the sanctioned player themselves doesn't return. This is a relatively recent change that trips up fans used to older rules.

name: Permitted Clothing
summary: Sets what players can legally wear on the field, covering safety and fairness.
what_it_says: Players wear a jersey, shorts, and boots as standard, with optional protective items like scrum caps, shoulder pads, and mouthguards permitted within set limits. Anything that could injure another player, such as exposed hard plastic or metal, is banned outright.
why_it_exists: In a full-contact sport, clothing and equipment can either protect players or become a hazard to others. This law draws that line clearly so equipment choices don't turn into a safety issue or an unfair advantage.
in_practice: Some players wear padded headgear, known as scrum caps, or thin shoulder padding under their jerseys, both legal and both offering modest protection without meaningfully changing how the game is played. Boot studs are also regulated, since illegal studs are a genuine injury risk in rucks and mauls.
common_confusions: Protective headgear in rugby doesn't work like a helmet in other contact sports. Scrum caps guard against cuts and cauliflower ear from scrums and rucks, not against concussion, which is a common point of confusion for people used to sports like American football.

name: Time
summary: Sets the length of a match and how stoppages are handled.
what_it_says: A full match is 80 minutes, split into two 40-minute halves, with time stopped for injuries, TMO reviews, and other significant stoppages. The referee, not a stadium clock, is the final authority on when time has actually elapsed.
why_it_exists: Rugby has frequent, sometimes lengthy stoppages, including injuries, scrum resets, and reviews, so a straightforward running clock wouldn't reflect actual playing time fairly. Giving the referee control over the clock keeps match length honest regardless of how many stoppages occur.
in_practice: A match often runs well past the 80-minute mark on the broadcast clock, because time stops for various delays and only resumes with play. A half doesn't end until the ball next goes dead after time has elapsed, which is why a team can keep attacking well past 40 or 80 minutes shown on screen.
common_confusions: The clock hitting 80 minutes doesn't end the match immediately. Play continues until the ball becomes dead, whether that's the ball going out, a try being scored, or a knock-on or penalty stopping it, which can extend a match by several minutes if a team keeps the ball alive.

name: Match Officials
summary: Defines the referee, assistant referees, and TMO, and their roles in controlling the match.
what_it_says: The referee has final authority over all decisions on the field, assisted by two assistant referees and, at higher levels, a Television Match Official (TMO) who reviews incidents using video replay. The TMO's role has expanded over time and now formally covers a defined set of decisions, including foul play and try-scoring incidents.
why_it_exists: A single on-field official can't see everything in a fast, physical game with players constantly grouped together. Assistant officials and the TMO exist to catch what the referee reasonably can't, particularly around player safety and close scoring decisions, without undermining the referee's overall control of the match.
in_practice: You'll hear the referee say things like TMO, please check that for a try, or see the big screen replay an incident while play is paused. The TMO doesn't make the final call in most cases, they advise, and the referee makes the actual decision, though for clear-cut incidents the TMO's recommendation is usually followed closely.
common_confusions: The TMO isn't reviewing every incident in the match, only specific categories of decision, mainly around tries, foul play, and time-sensitive safety issues. A missed forward pass several phases before a try, for example, generally isn't something the TMO goes hunting for unless it's directly in the passage of play being reviewed.

name: Advantage
summary: Lets play continue after an infringement if stopping it would unfairly help the team that broke the law.
what_it_says: When one team infringes, the referee can choose to let play continue if the non-offending team has a genuine chance to gain ground, territory, or tactical advantage, rather than stopping the game immediately for a penalty or scrum. If no advantage develops, play is brought back to the original infringement.
why_it_exists: Without advantage, stopping play for every single infringement would constantly reward the team that broke the law by handing them a dead-ball reset, and it would make the game stop-start and frustrating to watch. Advantage keeps the game flowing and lets genuine attacking opportunities play out.
in_practice: The referee calls advantage, often with an arm gesture, signalling they've seen an infringement but are letting play continue to see what happens. If the attacking team doesn't gain anything meaningful within a reasonable period, the referee brings it back for the original penalty or scrum.
common_confusions: Advantage doesn't last forever, and it isn't only about territory. A clear tactical advantage, such as quick clean possession to attack with, can count even without much ground gained. It's also possible for a team to gain advantage and then lose it again, in which case the referee can still bring play back if it happens quickly enough.

name: Scoring
summary: Sets out how points are earned through tries, conversions, penalty kicks, and drop goals.
what_it_says: A try is worth 5 points and is scored by grounding the ball in the opposition's in-goal area. A successful conversion kick afterward adds 2 points, a penalty kick at goal is worth 3, and a drop goal during open play is also worth 3.
why_it_exists: Different scoring methods reward different parts of the game. Straightforward tries reward attacking play and territory, while penalty and drop goals give a team a way to convert dominance or defensive discipline into points without needing to cross the try line. Weighting tries highest keeps attacking rugby the most valuable currency in the sport.
in_practice: Conversions are taken from a spot in line with where the try was scored, which is why tries near the posts are easier to convert than ones scored near the touchline. A well-worked try wide out is still worth the full 5 points, but the extra 2 from the conversion becomes much harder to land.
common_confusions: A penalty try is a specific, separate outcome, awarded when foul play clearly prevents a probable try, and is worth the same 5 points without needing to be physically grounded, since the offending team's actions are what stopped it happening.

name: Foul Play
summary: Dangerous, unfair, or unsporting actions that go beyond normal, physical rugby.
what_it_says: Foul play covers things like dangerous tackles, striking, tripping, and any contact that unfairly or dangerously targets an opponent, particularly around the head and neck. Depending on severity, it's penalised with a penalty kick, a yellow card for a temporary sin-bin, or a red card for permanent removal from the match.
why_it_exists: Rugby is a genuinely physical, contact-heavy sport, and this law exists to draw a clear line between hard, fair physicality and actions that put player safety at serious risk. As understanding of injuries, especially concussion, has grown, this law and its enforcement have become one of the most actively developed parts of the whole rulebook.
in_practice: Referees and, at higher levels, the TMO assess contact using a framework that looks closely at things like tackle height, whether the tackler was upright or bent at the point of contact, and whether the head was targeted or simply an unfortunate outcome of a legal tackle attempt. High, reckless, or head-on-head contact tends to draw the most severe sanctions, even without clear intent to injure.
common_confusions: A penalty for foul play doesn't require intent to hurt someone. A genuinely accidental but high or dangerous tackle can still be sanctioned, because the law is built around the risk created, not just what the player meant to do. Card decisions can also be reviewed and, in some competitions, upgraded or downgraded after the match through a judicial process, so a card shown on the day isn't always the final word on the incident.

name: Offside and Onside in Open Play
summary: A player is offside if they're ahead of a teammate who last played the ball.
what_it_says: If you're standing closer to the opposition's try line than the teammate who's carrying the ball, or who last touched it, you're offside. If the ball was last kicked, the offside line is drawn from wherever the kicker's foot made contact, not from where the kicker happens to be standing.
why_it_exists: Rugby needs space to work. If attackers could just stand next to the try line waiting for a pass, and defenders had no rule stopping them from swarming ahead of the ball, the game would collapse into chaos with no room to run, pass, or tackle. Offside is what keeps players tied to the actual contest instead of camping out for an easy score or an easy tackle.
in_practice: Standing in an offside position isn't a crime on its own, it happens constantly during open play and nobody blows a whistle for it. The penalty only comes if that player then does something: touches the ball, tackles the ball carrier, or blocks an opponent from playing. That's why a player who realises they're offside will throw their hands up and back away, showing the ref they're staying out of it, which is completely legal.
common_confusions: This applies to attackers just as much as defenders, any time you're ahead of the ball, not just defenders camped near the try line. It also gets mixed up with the separate offside rules at rucks, mauls, scrums, and lineouts, which have their own lines and distances. This law only covers open play.

name: Knock Forward or Throw Forward
summary: The ball can't be passed or knocked forward toward the opposition's try line.
what_it_says: A throw forward happens when the ball is passed toward the opponents' try line. A knock-on happens when the ball hits a player's hand or arm and goes forward, then touches the ground or another player before the original player catches it again. Either one stops play and results in a scrum to the non-offending team.
why_it_exists: Rugby is built around backward and lateral passing, which is what forces teams to work the ball across the width of the field rather than simply hurling it forward. This law is what makes rugby, structurally, a different game from something like American football or basketball, since territory has to be earned by running or kicking, not thrown.
in_practice: A ball that's fumbled and bounces backward isn't a knock-on, since it didn't go forward. A pass that drifts forward because of a player's own running line, rather than the pass itself going forward relative to the field, is usually fine too, since referees judge the ball's direction relative to the pitch, not the passer's body position. Most knock-ons are simple: a bad take at the breakdown, a dropped high ball, contact that pops the ball loose forward.
common_confusions: A knock-on only counts if the ball actually goes forward off the hand or arm. If it comes off a player's chest or leg and goes forward, that's not a knock-on under this law. An accidental knock-on that happens the instant a player is tackled, with no real advantage gained, is sometimes played on by the referee under advantage rather than stopped immediately.

name: Kick-off and Restart Kicks
summary: Governs how play restarts after scores and at the start of each half.
what_it_says: The match and each half start with a kick-off from the halfway line, and play restarts the same way after a try or successful goal, taken by the team that was scored against. The ball must travel at least 10 metres and land in the field of play, or the opposition can choose to have the kick redone or take a scrum.
why_it_exists: A consistent restart method keeps the game fair after a score, giving the team that conceded a chance to contest possession immediately rather than the scoring team simply keeping the ball. The 10-metre rule stops a team from tapping the ball a token distance just to retain possession unfairly.
in_practice: Teams often use restarts tactically, kicking long to pin the opposition deep or short to contest the ball in the air. A restart that doesn't reach 10 metres and is touched by the receiving team can be taken again, or turned into a scrum at the receiving team's choice.
common_confusions: A kick-off that goes directly into touch without bouncing isn't simply play-on. The receiving team gets a choice of options, including a scrum on halfway, which is often the more attractive choice for the team that would otherwise have had to defend a contestable kick.

name: Players on the Ground in Open Play
summary: Sets what a player on the ground can and can't do when there's no ruck or maul.
what_it_says: A player on the ground in open play, outside of a ruck or maul, must get up or move away before playing the ball again, and can't deliberately stay down to slow the game or block an opponent. They also can't be tackled again once genuinely on the ground and not playing the ball.
why_it_exists: Without this law, players could use their own body on the ground as an obstruction, slowing down defenders or attackers without any real contest for the ball taking place. It keeps play flowing by making sure grounded players either get involved properly or get out of the way.
in_practice: This shows up most after a tackle that doesn't immediately form a ruck. If the ball squirts loose, any player on the ground nearby has to act fast, either playing it fairly or clearing out of the space rather than lying over it.
common_confusions: This law is often confused with the tackle law itself, but it specifically covers players on the ground away from an actual tackle situation, such as loose ball scenarios and players who've simply slipped, where no formal ruck or maul has formed.

name: Tackle
summary: When a ball carrier is held and brought to ground by one or more opponents.
what_it_says: A tackle happens when the ball carrier is held by an opponent and brought to the ground. Once tackled, the ball carrier must immediately release the ball, and the tackler must immediately release the ball carrier and get up or move away before playing again.
why_it_exists: Without clear rules here, tackled players could just hold onto the ball indefinitely, and tacklers could pile on illegally. This law forces a quick release from both sides so the ball becomes available again fast, keeping the game moving instead of stalling in a heap on the ground.
in_practice: The moment the ball carrier is held and goes to ground, the clock is effectively running on how fast both players act. The tackled player has to let go of the ball right away and can't crawl forward with it. The tackler has to release and roll away, not stay draped over the ball carrier. Most tackle-area penalties are exactly these two things done too slowly, or a tackler diving in without properly binding.
common_confusions: The tackler can't simply hold the ball carrier down and fight for the ball from that position. Once the tackle's made, the tackler's job is to get out of the way, not compete for possession there. Competing for the ball after a tackle is what the ruck is for, not the tackle itself.

name: Ruck
summary: A contest for the ball on the ground, formed when players from both teams bind over it after a tackle.
what_it_says: A ruck forms when at least one player from each team is on their feet, in contact, and over the ball on the ground. Players can only join by binding onto a teammate or opponent already there, and once in the ruck, they can't use their hands on the ball.
why_it_exists: After a tackle, the ball needs a fair way to be contested and recycled rather than players just diving on it and holding it up indefinitely. The ruck lets both teams compete for it through pushing and clearing out, not grabbing, which keeps the game flowing and physical rather than turning every tackle into a wrestling match.
in_practice: Once a ruck has formed, hands off the ball, only feet can be used to move it. Players arriving late have to join from behind their own team's hindmost foot, not sideways or from the side, and can't dive over the top. Most penalties here come from hands in the ruck, sealing off the ball, or entering from the wrong side.
common_confusions: Not every pile-up after a tackle is a ruck. It isn't one until it meets the actual definition: players bound and on their feet over the ball. Before that point, a player on the ground can still be tackled or the ball can be played by hand, which is why a quick pick-and-go can happen before a ruck has properly formed.

name: Maul
summary: A moving contest for the ball involving the ball carrier and at least one player from each team, all on their feet.
what_it_says: A maul forms when the ball carrier is held by an opponent, and at least one more player from each team binds on, with everyone staying on their feet. Unlike a ruck, the ball is held in hand rather than on the ground, and the whole unit can move forward as a group.
why_it_exists: The maul lets a team keep driving forward with the ball in hand after contact, rather than being forced to release it to ground immediately. It rewards forward power and organisation, particularly off lineouts, and gives attacking teams a genuine way to grind out territory close to the try line.
in_practice: The maul can be pushed forward as a unit, and the ball can be shifted through hands within it as long as it stays off the ground. If the maul stops moving forward and the ball isn't available, the referee will call it and eventually award a scrum if nothing changes. Deliberately collapsing a maul, or bringing it down illegally, is a penalty, since it's a serious safety concern with players bound together and off balance.
common_confusions: A maul only exists once a second player from each team has bound onto the ball carrier while everyone stays upright. One attacker being held by one defender is still just a tackle situation, not a maul. If the maul goes to ground, it usually turns into a ruck instead, with different rules for who can play the ball.

name: Mark
summary: Lets a player catch the ball inside their own 22 and call an immediate, uncontested stop in play.
what_it_says: A player who catches the ball directly from an opponent's kick, while standing inside their own 22-metre area or in-goal, can call mark and be awarded a free kick on the spot, with no opposition pressure allowed at the moment of the catch.
why_it_exists: This exists to protect defending teams from being endlessly pressured by kicks into their own territory, giving them a safe, guaranteed way to reset play without needing to run the ball out under pressure every single time.
in_practice: A player shouts mark the instant they catch the ball, arm raised, and the referee stops play immediately. From there the team can either take a quick free kick or set up a more considered attacking option, without the opposition able to charge in and contest it.
common_confusions: A mark only counts on a direct catch from an opponent's kick, not from a teammate's kick, and not if the ball's touched by anyone else first. It also has to happen inside the 22 or in-goal; the same catch anywhere else on the field doesn't qualify.

name: Touch, Quick Throw and Lineout
summary: When the ball or a player carrying it goes over the touchline, and how play restarts from there.
what_it_says: The ball is in touch when it, or a player carrying it, crosses the touchline. Play can restart either with a quick throw-in by the same team, taken with the ball that went out, or with a formal lineout where players from both teams line up and compete for a throw thrown straight down the middle.
why_it_exists: Without a clear out-of-bounds rule, teams could simply run the ball off the field to avoid being tackled, or contest possession in chaotic, unstructured ways along the sideline. The lineout turns a stoppage into its own organised contest, similar in spirit to the scrum, while the quick throw option keeps the game moving when a team wants to play on immediately.
in_practice: For a quick throw, the same ball has to be used, thrown from where it went into touch, with no other player touching it before the throw. For a lineout, the throw has to go straight and at least 5 metres, and players can be lifted by teammates to compete for it in the air. Since 2026, teams have also been able to pass the ball back into their own half before kicking for the 50:22, which rewards accurate kicking from deep by turning it into a lineout throw for the kicking team if the ball lands in the field of play and bounces into touch inside the opposition's 22.
common_confusions: Whether the ball is in touch depends on the ball itself or the ball carrier's feet touching the ground beyond the line, not just the ball crossing above it in the air, so a ball caught in the air before it would have landed out is still in play. The 50:22 is often thought of as a separate law on its own, but it actually sits inside this law as a specific kicking rule, not a standalone one.

name: Scrum
summary: A contest for the ball between the two packs of forwards, used to restart play after a minor stoppage.
what_it_says: Eight players from each team bind together and push against the opposing pack. The scrum-half feeds the ball in, and both packs compete to hook it back with their feet. The ball must come out the back for play to continue normally.
why_it_exists: A scrum restarts play after something minor goes wrong, like a knock-on or a forward pass, without just handing possession to whichever team didn't make the mistake. It's also one of the oldest and most physical parts of rugby, rewarding raw forward power and technique as its own distinct contest within the game.
in_practice: The referee calls the front rows to crouch and bind before the ball is fed in. Most penalties at scrum time come from the front row: someone popping up early, pulling an opponent down, or the scrum collapsing dangerously. Once the ball's out the back, the scrum-half or a forward picks it up and play continues as normal.
common_confusions: The team pushing hardest doesn't automatically win the ball. It's the team putting the ball in that's supposed to win it, since they control the feed and the hooker strikes for it. A scrum going backwards, or collapsing, usually means a penalty against the pushing or collapsing team, not automatic possession for the other side.

name: Penalty and Free-Kick
summary: Sets what a team can do after being awarded a penalty or free kick, and the difference between the two.
what_it_says: A penalty kick can be taken at goal for 3 points, kicked to touch for territory, or tapped and run immediately. A free kick offers similar options but can't be kicked directly at goal for points, and a kick to touch from a free kick doesn't result in a lineout throw for the kicking team the way a penalty does.
why_it_exists: Different offences carry different weight, so the law gives referees two tiers of sanction: free kicks for more minor, technical infringements, and penalties for more serious ones, each with a different, proportionate set of options for the non-offending team.
in_practice: Teams choose their option based on the situation: kicking for goal when close enough and points matter, kicking to touch to gain territory and set up a lineout, or tapping and running quickly to catch a disorganised defence off guard.
common_confusions: A free kick and a penalty are often assumed to be interchangeable, but only a penalty can be kicked directly at the posts for points. Mixing the two up is a common source of confusion when trying to follow why a team did or didn't go for goal.

name: In-Goal
summary: Covers the area behind each try line and how tries, touchdowns, and dead-ball situations are handled there.
what_it_says: The in-goal area is the space behind each try line where tries are scored by grounding the ball. If a defending player grounds the ball in their own in-goal under pressure, or it becomes dead there without a try, play typically restarts with a drop-out rather than a scrum.
why_it_exists: The in-goal area needs its own clear rules since it's where matches are actually won and lost, and because defenders are often forced back into this zone under pressure, needing a fair, defined way to handle balls that end up there without a try being scored.
in_practice: A common sight is a chasing team pressuring a kick into the in-goal, forcing the defending team to either ground it themselves for a drop-out or attempt to run it out under heavy pressure. Since the 2026 law updates, several in-goal scenarios that don't result in a try now restart with a Try Line Drop-Out rather than the older 22 drop-out, changing how teams approach defending deep kicks.
common_confusions: Grounding the ball in your own in-goal isn't a try for the opposition and isn't inherently a bad outcome. It's simply a way to safely end that phase of play and restart with a drop-out, and is often the sensible choice under heavy pressure rather than risking a turnover or penalty try.
